title: Letter 12 — Do Unto Others as You Would Have Them Do Unto You
attribution_note: Letter 12 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

pairs.en: Let us listen to what Christ our Lord says to us: *“And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise”* [Luke 6:31]. From this it follows, O man, that what you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another; and what you wish for yourself, that do also to another.

sections.heading: What you do not want for yourself

pairs.en: You do not want anyone to wrong you, slander you, condemn you, revile you, dishonour you, seduce you, deceive you, beat you, wound you, kill you, hate you, be angry with you, take vengeance on you for his own hurt, drag you into court, or in any other way, by word or by deed, avenge himself upon you — you do not want any of this for yourself. You do not want anyone to defile your bed, to seize your wealth, to steal it, to take anything of yours against your will and make it his own — you do not want this; and how then can you wish evil upon yourself? Do not, then, O man, do to anyone what you do not wish for yourself; for he too does not wish for himself what you do not wish for yourself.

You wish that no one should leave you in your need — that is, that someone should feed you when you are hungry, clothe you when you are naked, visit and serve you when you are sick and in prison, take the stranger into his house and give him rest, build you a hut when you have no home, forgive you when you have sinned and bear with the wrong you did him, and so forth; you wish for all this — and how then can you not wish for good? Do, then, O man, for another what you wish for yourself; for he too wishes it for himself.

This the law of God, and the prophets, and the apostles teach us, according to the word of the Lord: *“for this is the law and the prophets”* [Matthew 7:12]. For the law, and the prophets, and the apostles teach us to turn away from evil and to do good, as their holy books bear witness. To this the holy fathers also, the pastors and teachers of the Church, exhort us, as we see in their writings.

It follows, then, that whoever does wrong to his neighbour, as set forth in the first point, does to him what he does not wish for himself; and so he is sick with self-love and walks in blindness, and does not know himself what he is doing, and fills his conscience with sins. And whoever does not help another in his need, as was said in the second point, though he is able to help, does not do for another what he wishes for himself; and he too is a lover of self and blind, and burdens his conscience — for which he will be convicted by his own conscience at the second coming of Christ, and will be left without excuse. Therefore we read that by Christ the righteous Judge those are sent away into the fire who showed no mercy to the least of His brethren, that is, to Christians in distress [Matthew 25:41, 45].

Therefore without excuse will be the miserly rich, who do not help the poor out of their wealth, but squander their wealth on their own pleasures — on costly buildings, on rich tables, and the like — or else hoard it in their coffers, and keep it like watchmen guarding a post; without excuse are those who do not take the stranger into their homes, and all the rest who show no mercy to their neighbour; for all such do not do for their neighbour what they wish for themselves.

sections.heading: Turn from evil and do good

pairs.en: Let us listen, O Christians, to the prophets, the apostles, the teachers of the Church, and above all to Christ our God Himself, who through them instructs and exhorts us; let us bring forth true repentance, and, *“depart from evil, and do good”* [Psalm 33:15]; and having begun to do good, let us abide in it to the end, that death may find us in it, and so we may be saved by the grace of Christ. For he who has begun, but has not endured to the end, will not be saved. *“But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved,”* according to the teaching of Christ [Matthew 24:13].

To those who have begun to do good, and are doing it, the apostle says: *“let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not”* [Galatians 6:9]. The present time is the time of sowing, but there will be a time of harvest — that is, the time of the resurrection from the dead. Then everyone will reap whatever he now sows. Just as the farmer reaps, from whatever seed he sows, the crop that grows up from it — whether he sows rye, or wheat, or oats, or anything else, such is the crop he reaps — so the Christian, whatever seeds he now sows, that is, good deeds or evil, such will be the crop he reaps at the time of the resurrection; as the apostle says: *“For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting”* [Galatians 6:8]; and in another place: *“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord”* [Romans 6:23; Matthew 25]. Let us turn aside, then, beloved, from the carnal passions that war against our soul, and let us bring forth *“works meet for repentance”* [Acts 26:20] — good works — that we may reap our fruit in the resurrection of the just. Then we shall be *“recompensed”* richly from the hand of the Lord [Luke 14:14].

The apostle says further: *“As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith”* [Galatians 6:10]. What does this mean — “while we have time”?

Answer. The present, the now, while we live in this world, is the time for doing good — not the future, after death, for then will be the time of recompense. Whatever a man has done here, while living in the world — good or evil — with that he will appear at the judgment of Christ. Then *“every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad,”* as the apostle teaches [2 Corinthians 5:10]. But after death the doing of good will cease; then there will be recompense to every man according to his deeds. Therefore the present time is likened to sowing, and the future to the harvest.

Farmers sow their seed, but by the blessing of God they gather in a far greater crop, as we see. So devout souls do good works in the name of the Lord, but for those works they will receive from the hand of the Lord, in the life to come, a hundredfold recompense, as an abundant harvest.
Farmers rejoice when they gather in the crop of the seed they have sown; so Christians, who now sow the seed of good works, will reap with joy the fruit of their blessed labours.

Lazy farmers and idlers are left without a crop at harvest time, because they did not labour, they did not sow, but lay about or went idly roaming during the sowing season; and so they are left in poverty and shame, and, seeing the others — their own brethren — gathering in their crops and rejoicing, they grieve, and curse themselves. The same will befall Christians who let the present time slip by and do no good, but spend this time on revelry, amusements, feasting, and other pleasures — things displeasing to God and harmful to themselves; they too will be put to shame at the second coming of Christ, and, seeing themselves in utter and eternal poverty, wretchedness and misery, while the rest are in eternal blessedness, they will weep bitterly and lament — lament, seeing themselves poor and wretched, though in this world they were rich and glorious. *“Therefore have we erred from the way of truth: and the light of righteousness hath not shined unto us, and the sun of righteousness rose not upon us.* *We wearied ourselves in the way of wickedness and destruction: yea, we have gone through deserts where there lay no way: but as for the way of the Lord, we have not known it.* *What hath pride profited us? or what good hath riches with our vaunting done us?* *All those things are passed away like a shadow, and as a post that hasted by”* [Wisdom of Solomon 5:6–9]. Let us be likened, then, beloved, to the diligent farmers, and let us sow, while we have time, the seed of good works, that in the life to come we may reap with joy, and a hundredfold, fruit that abides for ever and ever.
*“Let us do good unto all men,”* says the apostle. What does this word mean — “unto all”?

Answer. We must do good to all — to the good and to the evil, to friends and to enemies, to kinsmen and to strangers, to countrymen and to foreigners — in a word, to every man, whoever asks of us and seeks anything from us, as Christ says: *“Give to every man that asketh of thee”* [Luke 6:30]. Let us, then, O Christians, do good to all, that we may be true Christians, *“children of light”* [1 Thessalonians 5:5], the sons of our Father who is in heaven, *“for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust”* [Matthew 5:45] — to whom we pray every day: *“Our Father, which art in heaven”* [Matthew 6:9] — and let us do good according to our strength and ability. If we have much, let us give much; and if we have little, let us share and give even out of that little, as Tobias exhorts [Tobit 4:8], that both for the little and for the great we may receive a hundredfold from our God, who is generous and rich in mercy.
